runtime.title: Scalars, vectors and interactions
runtime.big: Scalars have magnitude only: distance, speed, mass, time and energy. Vectors also have direction: displacement, velocity, acceleration and force. An arrow shows direction; its length represents magnitude using a stated scale. Turning a velocity arrow changes velocity even when its length stays the same.

learn.title: Magnitude and direction
learn.text: Scalars have magnitude only: distance, speed, mass, time and energy. Vectors also have direction: displacement, velocity, acceleration and force. An arrow shows direction; its length represents magnitude using a stated scale. Turning a velocity arrow changes velocity even when its length stays the same.

learn.title: Two objects, two forces
learn.text: A force is a push or pull arising from an interaction. Contact interactions include friction, air resistance, tension and normal contact. Gravity, electrostatic and magnetic interactions act without physical contact. Each object exerts a force on the other; name the objects and what acts on what.

learn.title: Read a scaled arrow
learn.text: With 1 cm representing 5 N, a 3 cm arrow represents 15 N in the arrow’s direction. Reversing the arrow reverses the represented force; it does not make its magnitude negative. A signed number can encode direction along a chosen straight-line axis.

runtime.title: Mass, weight and gravity
runtime.big: Mass measures the amount of matter in kilograms; weight is the gravitational force in newtons. A gravitational field gives objects weight even when there is no contact. Moving an object to a different field changes its weight while its mass can remain unchanged.

learn.title: Mass is not a force
learn.text: Mass measures the amount of matter in kilograms; weight is the gravitational force in newtons. A gravitational field gives objects weight even when there is no contact. Moving an object to a different field changes its weight while its mass can remain unchanged.

learn.title: Use W = mg
learn.text: Weight W = mass m × field strength g. Use the supplied g in N/kg. For 3 kg with g=9.8 N/kg, W=29.4 N. Weight is directly proportional to mass at fixed g. A calibrated newtonmeter measures weight, not kilograms of mass.

learn.title: Centre of mass
learn.text: For force diagrams, the weight can be represented as acting through the centre of mass toward the attracting body. The marker is a simplified whole-object representation, not a statement that all the object’s matter lies at one point.

learn.title: Compare fields
learn.text: Choose mass and gravitational field strength. Predict the newtonmeter reading, then reveal. The downward arrow changes in proportion to mg. The demonstration is stationary; support balances weight, and no fall-time calculation is implied.

learn.title: Zero resultant does not mean no forces

learn.title: Avoid mixing objects

runtime.title: Work done by a force
runtime.big: A force does work when it causes displacement along its line of action. Work done W=Fs, with force in N and distance along that force in m. The result is energy transferred in joules. One joule equals one newton-metre of work.

learn.title: Force through a displacement
learn.text: A force does work when it causes displacement along its line of action. Work done W=Fs, with force in N and distance along that force in m. The result is energy transferred in joules. One joule equals one newton-metre of work.

learn.title: Keep the direction condition
learn.text: A 20 N force acting through3 m along its direction transfers60 J. A sideways force with no displacement along it does not transfer work through that sideways component. A large static force with zero displacement does no mechanical work on the stationary object.

learn.title: Friction transfers energy
learn.text: Work done against friction reduces mechanical energy stores and raises internal energy/temperature of the object and surroundings. Energy is conserved even when the useful mechanical transfer is smaller than the input. Use the existing Energy lessons for the linked store account.

runtime.title: Elasticity and force–extension graphs
runtime.big: A stationary object needs opposing applied forces to stretch, bend or compress it. Elastic deformation reverses when forces are removed. Inelastic deformation leaves a permanent change. The limit of proportionality marks where a force–extension graph stops being a straight line through the origin; it is not a universal synonym for the elastic limit.

learn.title: Two forces change shape
learn.text: A stationary object needs opposing applied forces to stretch, bend or compress it. Elastic deformation reverses when forces are removed. Inelastic deformation leaves a permanent change. The limit of proportionality marks where a force–extension graph stops being a straight line through the origin; it is not a universal synonym for the elastic limit.

learn.title: Use F = ke in the linear region
learn.text: Extension e = stretched length − original length, in metres. Spring constant k is force per unit extension, N/m. A spring with k=100 N/m under5 N extends0.05 m. Compression can be treated similarly. A steeper F-versus-e gradient means a larger k.

learn.title: Energy stored while stretching
learn.text: If the spring stays within the proportional elastic region, elastic energy E=½ke² equals work done stretching it. The force increases with extension, so multiplying the final force by extension overestimates the work. The energy is the triangular area under the F–e graph.

learn.title: Stretch two ideal springs
learn.text: Choose k and applied force, predict extension, then reveal. The model stays in the stated linear elastic region and returns to its original length on unloading. Coil thickness/diameter are symbolic; the spring is not a material-failure prediction.

runtime.title: Moments, levers and gears
runtime.big: Moment M=F d, where d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force’s line of action. Use N m. A longer lever arm can produce the same moment with a smaller force. A force directed through the pivot has zero moment even if applied far along the lever.

learn.title: A turning effect
learn.text: Moment M=F d, where d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force’s line of action. Use N m. A longer lever arm can produce the same moment with a smaller force. A force directed through the pivot has zero moment even if applied far along the lever.

learn.title: Balance clockwise and anticlockwise
learn.text: A balanced object has equal total clockwise and anticlockwise moments about the pivot. A6 N downward force0.2 m left balances a3 N downward force0.4 m right: both moments are1.2 N m. Include every force with a moment, not just one pair.

learn.title: Transmit rotation
learn.text: Levers transmit turning effects. Meshing gears rotate in opposite directions; a smaller gear turns through more revolutions than a larger meshing gear. Changing gear sizes changes turning effect/speed tradeoffs. A simple ideal gear train transfers energy; it does not create energy.

runtime.big: The pressure due to a liquid column is p=hρg. Use column height/depth h in m, densityρ in kg/m³ and supplied g in N/kg. This is the additional liquid pressure; add surface pressure if asked for absolute pressure. Denser liquid or greater depth gives larger pressure.

learn.title: Pressure increases with depth
learn.text: The pressure due to a liquid column is p=hρg. Use column height/depth h in m, densityρ in kg/m³ and supplied g in N/kg. This is the additional liquid pressure; add surface pressure if asked for absolute pressure. Denser liquid or greater depth gives larger pressure.

learn.title: A pressure difference gives upthrust
learn.text: A submerged object has greater pressure on its bottom than its top. The vertical force difference gives upward upthrust; opposing horizontal forces can cancel. Upthrust depends on displaced fluid. The diagram exaggerates vertical pressure differences for clarity.

learn.title: Float or sink
learn.text: An unsupported object initially sinks if weight exceeds upthrust and rises if upthrust exceeds weight. It floats at rest when upthrust balances weight. A floating object displaces its own weight of fluid. Average object density and fluid density help decide whether it can float; shape affects the displaced volume.

runtime.title: Atmospheric pressure and altitude
runtime.big: The atmosphere is a thin layer compared with Earth’s size. Air molecules continually move and collide with surfaces, producing atmospheric pressure. The atmosphere is denser closer to the ground and becomes less dense at higher altitudes.

learn.title: A thin layer around Earth
learn.text: The atmosphere is a thin layer compared with Earth’s size. Air molecules continually move and collide with surfaces, producing atmospheric pressure. The atmosphere is denser closer to the ground and becomes less dense at higher altitudes.

learn.title: Less air above
learn.text: At a higher altitude there are fewer air molecules and less weight of air above each unit area. Atmospheric pressure therefore decreases with altitude. Pressure does not suddenly become zero at the top of a building; the change depends on the height and atmospheric conditions.

learn.title: Use evidence carefully
learn.text: Compare measured pressure at different heights while considering weather changes and instrument calibration. The gas particles are greatly enlarged and only a few are drawn. Their collisions represent a mechanism, not a literal number of air molecules.

runtime.title: Distance, displacement, speed and velocity
runtime.big: Distance is total path length, a scalar. Displacement is the straight-line change from start to finish with direction, a vector. Walk3 m east then3 m west: distance6 m, displacement0. Speed is scalar; velocity is speed in a stated direction.

learn.title: A journey has two measures
learn.text: Distance is total path length, a scalar. Displacement is the straight-line change from start to finish with direction, a vector. Walk3 m east then3 m west: distance6 m, displacement0. Speed is scalar; velocity is speed in a stated direction.

learn.title: Use distance = speed × time
learn.text: For constant speed, s=vt. Average speed for a variable journey is total distance divided by total time, including stated stops. Do not simply average two speeds unless the time intervals are equal. Convert km/h to m/s by dividing by3.6.

learn.title: Estimate sensible speeds
learn.text: Typical walking speed is1.5 m/s, running3 m/s, cycling6 m/s and sound in air about330 m/s. Terrain, fitness, age and journey length affect human speeds. A car on a road may travel around13 m/s (about30 mph), while other transport varies widely. These are estimates, not universal constants.

learn.title: Compare simple journeys
learn.text: Choose constant speed and elapsed time. Predict total distance before watching a straight-line journey. The markers show equally spaced positions for equal times. A later return leg can change displacement without undoing the distance already travelled.

learn.title: Higher: constant speed can still change velocity
learn.text: An object moving in a circle changes direction continuously even at constant speed. Its velocity changes, so it accelerates. The resultant force is toward the centre; it is perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity, not a force pushing the object outward.

runtime.title: Reading distance–time graphs
runtime.big: On a distance–time graph, gradient = change in distance ÷ change in time. A steeper positive line means greater speed. A horizontal section means no further distance travelled during that time. A straight sloping line represents constant speed.

learn.title: A slope tells you speed
learn.text: On a distance–time graph, gradient = change in distance ÷ change in time. A steeper positive line means greater speed. A horizontal section means no further distance travelled during that time. A straight sloping line represents constant speed.

learn.title: Construct from measurements
learn.text: Choose sensible axis ranges, plot time horizontally and distance vertically with units, and plot measured points. A line or smooth curve should fit the evidence. Use a large gradient triangle, reading two points on the line rather than assuming it starts at the origin.

learn.title: Curves represent changing speed
learn.text: A curve getting steeper represents increasing speed; a curve getting flatter represents decreasing speed. Total distance cannot decrease in a cumulative-distance account. A position/displacement graph can decrease, but that is a different vertical quantity.

learn.title: Compare slopes
learn.text: Choose a distance increment and time interval; predict gradient in m/s and reveal the graph. This is constrained graph interpretation. It prepares for drawing and analysing your own measured graph, but does not itself provide unrestricted graph-construction evidence.

learn.title: Higher: measure a tangent
learn.text: For instantaneous speed on a curved distance–time graph, draw a tangent at the chosen time and calculate its gradient using a large triangle on that tangent. Do not use the chord joining widely separated curve points. A tangent rising12 m over4 s gives3 m/s at the contact point.

runtime.title: Acceleration and uniform-motion calculations

learn.title: Velocity changes per second
learn.text: Average acceleration a=(v−u)/t. Units are m/s². Choose a positive direction first. A vehicle changing from2 to14 m/s in4 s has acceleration3 m/s². Slowing while moving in the positive direction gives negative acceleration; the magnitude of deceleration is positive.

learn.title: A second relationship
learn.text: For uniform acceleration, v²−u²=2as. Rearrange carefully and use SI units. With u=0, a=2 m/s² and s=9 m, v²=36 and speed=6 m/s. The relationship assumes constant acceleration; it cannot be applied indiscriminately to a whole nonuniform journey.

learn.title: Free fall and resistance

runtime.title: Falling objects and terminal velocity
runtime.big: A falling object initially has weight greater than air resistance, so it accelerates downward. As speed increases, air resistance rises and the downward resultant decreases. Weight remains approximately constant for the same mass and gravitational field.

learn.title: Forces change during a fall
learn.text: A falling object initially has weight greater than air resistance, so it accelerates downward. As speed increases, air resistance rises and the downward resultant decreases. Weight remains approximately constant for the same mass and gravitational field.

learn.title: Reach a balanced speed
learn.text: At terminal velocity, drag balances weight and resultant force is zero. Acceleration is zero, but the object is still moving. A larger drag at a given speed, such as an opened parachute, can give a lower terminal speed. Immediately after opening, upward drag can exceed weight and the falling object slows.

runtime.title: Newton’s first law and inertia
runtime.big: If the resultant force is zero, a stationary object stays at rest and a moving object continues at the same speed in the same direction. A force is needed to change velocity, not to keep an ideal object moving at constant velocity.

learn.title: Keep a constant velocity
learn.text: If the resultant force is zero, a stationary object stays at rest and a moving object continues at the same speed in the same direction. A force is needed to change velocity, not to keep an ideal object moving at constant velocity.

learn.title: Balance a real vehicle
learn.text: A car at steady speed has drive balancing resistance. Turning a corner changes direction and therefore velocity, so it requires a resultant even if speed stays the same. Friction explains why everyday coasting objects slow when drive is removed.

learn.title: Explain the interaction
learn.text: Identify the chosen object and all important forces on it. Ask whether the vector sum is zero. A book resting on a table has balanced support and weight on the book; these are not Newton’s third-law partners because both act on the same object.

learn.title: Higher: inertia
learn.text: Inertia is the tendency of an object to remain at rest or continue in uniform straight-line motion. It does not mean a new force pushes the object forward. When a bus brakes, an unrestrained passenger tends to keep moving; a restraint exerts a force to change that motion.

runtime.title: Newton’s second law
runtime.big: F=ma links resultant force in N, mass in kg and acceleration in m/s². The acceleration is in the resultant force’s direction. Use the resultant, not just the driving force when resistance is present.

learn.text: At fixed mass, acceleration is proportional to resultant force. At fixed resultant force it is inversely proportional to mass: doubling mass halves acceleration. A6 N resultant on2 kg gives3 m/s². The proportionality symbol is ∝.

learn.title: Interactions come in pairs

runtime.title: Thinking distance, reaction time and stopping
runtime.short: Thinking distance, reaction time and stopping
runtime.big: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. During reaction time the vehicle is still travelling before braking begins. At roughly constant speed, thinking distance = speed × reaction time. Braking distance begins when the brakes act.

learn.title: Two parts of stopping
learn.text: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. During reaction time the vehicle is still travelling before braking begins. At roughly constant speed, thinking distance = speed × reaction time. Braking distance begins when the brakes act.

learn.title: Reaction time varies
learn.text: Typical human reaction times are about0.2–0.9 s. Tiredness, drugs/alcohol and distractions can increase reaction time. Measure with a ruler-drop test or a computer/light response test; control anticipation and practise effects, repeat and compare variability. A ruler measures fall distance, which must be converted to time using a supplied relationship.

learn.title: Road and vehicle conditions
learn.text: Wet/icy roads and poor tyres/brakes can increase braking distance by reducing effective braking. They need not increase the driver’s intrinsic reaction time. Higher speed increases thinking distance and usually braking distance. Compare supplied emergency-stop graphs for different vehicles/conditions; values are not interchangeable universal rules.

runtime.title: Braking, energy and deceleration
runtime.big: Brake friction transfers energy from the vehicle’s kinetic store to internal energy of brakes and surroundings; brake temperature rises. Work done by an approximately constant braking force is Fs. Setting that equal to½mv² gives an ideal stopping-energy account.

learn.title: Transfer kinetic energy
learn.text: Brake friction transfers energy from the vehicle’s kinetic store to internal energy of brakes and surroundings; brake temperature rises. Work done by an approximately constant braking force is Fs. Setting that equal to½mv² gives an ideal stopping-energy account.

learn.title: Speed matters strongly
learn.text: For fixed mass and braking force, doubling speed gives four times the initial kinetic energy and four times the ideal braking distance. Real road grip, brake/tyre condition and weather alter the available force. These assumptions must be stated when interpreting a squared-speed trend.

learn.title: Deceleration and control
learn.text: For a given distance, greater speed requires greater braking force. Larger braking force gives larger deceleration. Very large deceleration can cause loss of control and brakes can overheat. A generated energy comparison cannot establish safe stopping distances for a real journey.

runtime.title: Momentum and conservation
runtime.big: Momentum p=mv, in kg m/s. It is a vector, so choose positive direction and include signs. A2 kg trolley at3 m/s has momentum6 kg m/s. Equal speeds do not imply equal momentum if masses differ.

learn.title: Mass times velocity
learn.text: Momentum p=mv, in kg m/s. It is a vector, so choose positive direction and include signs. A2 kg trolley at3 m/s has momentum6 kg m/s. Equal speeds do not imply equal momentum if masses differ.

learn.title: Define the closed system
learn.text: Total momentum before an event equals total momentum after if the system has no resultant external force during it. The interaction forces between objects are internal; they redistribute momentum without changing the system total. Momentum conservation does not require kinetic energy conservation in every collision.

learn.title: Explain a collision
learn.text: If a moving trolley hits a stationary one, momentum can transfer to it. In a sticking collision the combined mass moves more slowly than the original trolley for equal masses. In explosions, opposite signed momenta can sum to the initial total. Direction signs prevent adding magnitudes incorrectly.

learn.text: Choose mass and signed velocity. Predict momentum and reveal a moving trolley with an arrow in its velocity direction. The demonstration isolates p=mv; the loop does not simulate an elastic collision law. Numerical two-object collision solving is reserved for the separate-Physics extension.

runtime.title: Calculating collision and recoil momentum

learn.title: A sticking example
learn.text: A2 kg trolley at3 m/s sticks to a stationary4 kg trolley. Initial momentum6 kg m/s equals6v afterwards, so v=1 m/s. Check that units are kg m/s and final velocity is plausible. Kinetic energy decreases; momentum still balances.

learn.title: Recoil and opposite directions
learn.text: An initially stationary system has total momentum zero. If a1 kg object leaves at+4 m/s, the remaining2 kg must have−4 kg m/s and velocity−2 m/s. Opposite signs matter; do not conserve scalar speeds. Real external forces may make a chosen system only approximately isolated.

runtime.title: Force, momentum change and protection
runtime.big: A resultant force changes momentum. Average force F=Δp/Δt, in newtons. Use final momentum minus initial momentum and a consistent positive direction. A2 kg object slowing from10 m/s to rest changes momentum by−20 kg m/s.

learn.title: Change momentum over time
learn.text: A resultant force changes momentum. Average force F=Δp/Δt, in newtons. Use final momentum minus initial momentum and a consistent positive direction. A2 kg object slowing from10 m/s to rest changes momentum by−20 kg m/s.

learn.title: Spread the change over longer time
learn.text: For the same momentum change, increasing collision time reduces average force. Seat belts, airbags, crumple zones and landing mats increase stopping time/distance while restraining or cushioning motion. They do not remove the momentum change required to stop an object.

learn.title: Evaluate a protection claim
learn.text: A force calculated from Δp/Δt is an average, not necessarily the peak. Compare supplied time, force and injury-related evidence; a longer stopping interval alone does not guarantee every outcome. Protection must restrain the object effectively and avoid additional hazards.

learn.title: Compare two stopping times
learn.text: A toy object of2 kg stops from a selected speed. Choose stopping time and predict force magnitude2v/t. The animation stretches the stopping sequence for clarity. It is not a crash-test body model or a design certification.

practice.why: Average resultant force is the signed change in momentum divided by the stopping interval.
